title: VC Dimension of Specific Hypothesis Classes
description: Computes the VC dimension of three hypothesis classes: powerset (shatters all), threshold classifiers (VCDim = 1), and interval classifiers (VCDim = 2). The interval result uses a convexity argument: if a < b < c and both a,c lie in [lo,hi), then b must also lie in [lo,hi), making {a,c} unrealizable.

overview.historicalContext: The Vapnik-Chervonenkis (VC) dimension, introduced in 1971, is the central combinatorial parameter in statistical learning theory. It measures the expressive power of a hypothesis class by the size of the largest set it can shatter (label in all 2^n possible ways). Computing the VC dimension of specific hypothesis classes is fundamental: threshold classifiers have VCDim 1 (they are monotone), interval classifiers have VCDim 2 (they are convex but not monotone), and d-dimensional halfspaces have VCDim d+1.
overview.problemStatement:
Compute the VC dimension of specific hypothesis classes:
1. **Powerset** $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$: VCDim = $|\Omega|$ (shatters every finite set)
2. **Threshold classifiers** $\{\{n : n < t\} : t \in \mathbb{N}\}$: VCDim = 1
3. **Interval classifiers** $\{\{n : lo \leq n < hi\} : lo, hi \in \mathbb{N}\}$: VCDim = 2
overview.text: Defines VC dimension for hypothesis classes and computes it for powerset (shatters all), thresholds (VCDim = 1), and intervals (VCDim = 2). The interval non-shattering uses convexity: if a < b < c with a,c in an interval, then b is too.
overview.proofStrategy:
For each hypothesis class, the VC dimension is established by proving both directions:

1. **Lower bound**: Exhibit a set of the claimed size that is shattered. For thresholds, any singleton {a} is shattered (empty set via t=0, full set via t=a+1). For intervals, any pair {a,b} is shattered (four intervals realize all four subsets).

2. **Upper bound**: Show no larger set can be shattered. For thresholds, monotonicity of {n < t} prevents realizing {b} from {a,b} when a < b (if b < t then a < t). For intervals, convexity prevents realizing {a,c} from {a,b,c} when a < b < c (if a,c in [lo,hi) then b in [lo,hi)).

The convexity argument for intervals is the key insight: intervals are connected subsets of the naturals, so they cannot separate non-adjacent elements while excluding elements between them.
keyInsights: Threshold classifiers have VCDim 1 because they are monotone: {n < t} is an initial segment, so including a larger element forces inclusion of all smaller ones
Interval classifiers have VCDim 2 because they are convex: [lo, hi) cannot contain endpoints a,c while excluding an intermediate point b
The powerset trivially shatters everything (VCDim = |domain|), establishing the maximum possible VC dimension
The non-shattering proofs are more interesting than the shattering proofs: they require identifying the specific unrealizable subset

sections.title: Core Definitions
sections.summary: Defines HypothesisClass (family of subsets), Shatters (every subset realizable), and vcDim (largest shattered set size).
sections.mathContext: $H$ shatters $S$ if $\forall T \subseteq S, \exists h \in H$ s.t. $h \cap S = T$. VCDim$(H) = \sup\{|S| : H \text{ shatters } S\}$.

sections.title: Powerset Shattering
sections.summary: The powerset (all subsets) shatters every finite set trivially: for any T, use h = T.
sections.mathContext: $\mathcal{P}(\Omega)$ shatters $S$ for all $S$: just take $h = T$ for any $T \subseteq S$.

sections.title: Threshold Classifiers: VCDim = 1
sections.summary: Threshold classifiers {n < t} shatter singletons but cannot shatter pairs. The non-shattering uses monotonicity: b < t forces a < t when a < b.
sections.mathContext: VCDim$\{\{n < t\}\} = 1$. Shatters $\{a\}$ (use $t=0$ and $t=a+1$). Cannot shatter $\{a,b\}$ with $a < b$: the subset $\{b\}$ requires $b < t$ and $a \geq t$, but $a < b < t$ contradicts $a \geq t$.

sections.title: Interval Classifiers: Shattering Pairs
sections.summary: Interval classifiers [lo, hi) shatter any pair {a, b} with a < b. Each of the four subsets is realized by an appropriate interval.

sections.title: Interval Classifiers: Non-Shattering of Triples
sections.summary: Interval classifiers cannot shatter any triple {a, b, c} with a < b < c. The subset {a, c} is unrealizable: if a,c are in [lo,hi), convexity forces b in [lo,hi) too.
sections.mathContext: For $a < b < c$: $\{a,c\}$ requires $a \in [lo,hi)$ and $c \in [lo,hi)$ but $b \notin [lo,hi)$. But $lo \leq a < b < c < hi$ forces $b \in [lo,hi)$. Contradiction.

crossReferences.description: This proof computes VC dimensions for specific classes; the parent proves the Sauer-Shelah lemma bounding growth functions in terms of VC dimension

conclusion.summary: Complete VC dimension computation for three fundamental hypothesis classes, establishing VCDim(powerset) = |domain|, VCDim(thresholds) = 1, and VCDim(intervals) = 2. The interval result uses a clean convexity argument that generalizes to any connected hypothesis class.
conclusion.implications: These concrete computations complement the abstract Sauer-Shelah bounds in the parent proof. They demonstrate that VC dimension captures geometric structure: monotone classes (thresholds) have lower VC dimension than convex classes (intervals), which have lower VC dimension than unrestricted classes (powerset).
openQuestions: What is the connection to Rademacher complexity, and can the Rademacher-based generalization bound be formalized?
VCDim for halfspace classifiers in R^d (expected: d+1) — requires formalizing linear algebra over R
Can the epsilon-net theorem be formalized in Lean to get the tighter sample complexity bound?
